title: Ordinary curve points characterized by delta and branch number
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], $X$ a reduced finite-type $k$-scheme of pure dimension one [def-pc-reduced-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism, def-weil-pure-dimension], and $x\in X(k)$ a closed point. Let $
u:\widetilde X	o X$ be the disjoint union of the normalizations of its reduced irreducible components [def-sc-normalization]. Put $b=|
u^{-1}(x)|$ and $\delta=\dim_k((
u_*\mathcal O_{\widetilde X})_x/\mathcal O_{X,x})$, using sheaf direct image on opens and the natural inclusion of local rings. These numbers are finite, $b\ge1$, and $\delta\ge b-1$. Equality holds if and only if the maximal-ideal completion [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion] is isomorphic as a $k$-algebra to
$$\widehat{\mathcal O}_{X,x}\cong k[[t_1,\ldots,t_b]]/(t_it_j\mid i
e j),$$
with formal power series as in [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. This condition is called an ordinary $b$-fold point. An ordinary one-fold point is exactly a smooth point [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]; an ordinary two-fold point is exactly an ordinary node. Thus smooth points have $\delta=0$, and nodes have $b=2$ and $\delta=1$.

source.place: Appendix B, ordinary n-fold points and the inequality/equality characterization preceding Lemma B.1, printed pp. 56--57. Primary PDF read online; local archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Work on an affine neighbourhood of $x$; restriction of componentwise normalization is normalization of that neighbourhood. The normalization theorem makes $\nu$ finite and surjective. The finite-fibres theorem therefore gives $1\le b<\infty$. A point $y_i$ above $x$ is closed: on the finite affine inverse image its prime contains the ideal of the fibre, and the corresponding quotient of the finite-dimensional $k$-algebra of the fibre is a finite-dimensional domain, hence a field (multiplication by a nonzero element is injective, hence surjective). The closed-point residue-field theorem gives $\kappa(y_i)=k$ through the structural map. Put $A=\mathcal O_{X,x}$, $B=(\nu_*\mathcal O_{\widetilde X})_x$ and $M=B/A$. The finite-type Noetherianity theorem makes $A$ Noetherian. It is reduced, essentially of finite type over $k$, and has dimension one: a component through $x$ supplies a generic-point-to-$x$ chain, and no longer chain exists on a pure one-dimensional scheme.

source.place: Tag 0C1R (lemma-prepare-delta-invariant), (1), (3); normalization restricted to an affine neighbourhood; finite fibres: morphisms.tex Tags 01WN, 02NU, 02NH; residue fields over algebraically closed fields.

proof.text: If $x$ is nonsmooth, the normalization-quotient theorem identifies $B$ with the integral closure of $A$ in its total ring of fractions and makes $M$ a finite-length $A$-module. If $x$ is smooth, the regularity/smoothness criterion applies to the finite-type affine chart with residue field $k$, hence $A$ is regular. Since $\dim A=1$, the regular/normal equivalence makes $A$ a normal domain. The normalization theorem's isomorphism over its open normal locus then gives $B=A$ and $M=0$. Thus in both cases $B$ is the integral closure of $A$ in its total ring of fractions and $M$ has finite length.

source.place: Tag 0C1R (lemma-prepare-delta-invariant), (2)--(4); smooth case: algebra.tex Tags 00TV (lemma-separable-smooth) and 00PD (lemma-characterize-dvr).

proof.text: The finite-length filtration theorem gives a finite filtration of $M$ with simple quotients. Each simple $A$-module is $k$: choose a nonzero element, whose cyclic submodule is the whole simple module; the resulting surjection from $A$ has maximal kernel, necessarily $\mathfrak m_A$. Adding dimensions along the filtration proves $\delta=\dim_k M<\infty$. Put $H=\widehat A$ and $C=\widehat B$, where $B$ is completed for $\mathfrak m_AB$. The local-curve normalization/completion theorem identifies $C=B\otimes_AH$ with the integral closure of the reduced one-dimensional ring $H$ in its total ring of fractions. For nonsmooth $x$, the normalization-quotient theorem gives the natural $k$-linear isomorphism $M\cong C/H$; its map is $A$-linear, hence respects the structural $k$-action. For smooth $x$, $B=A$, so $C=H$ and the same comparison is the zero-module isomorphism. Consequently $\delta=\dim_k(C/H)$.

source.place: Tags 0C1R (lemma-prepare-delta-invariant), (6)--(9), and 0C3V (lemma-normalization-same-after-completion); finite-algebra completion: algebra.tex Tag 07N9 (lemma-completion-finite-extension).

proof.text: The finite-algebra completion theorem, applied to the finite $A$-algebra $B$ at $\mathfrak m_A$, gives $C\cong\prod_{i=1}^b R_i$ with $R_i=\widehat{\mathcal O}_{\widetilde X,y_i}$, respecting the maps from $H$ and $B$. Each normalized irreducible component is smooth over the perfect field $k$, by the normalization-properties theorem. Choose an affine open neighbourhood of $y_i$ in that integral component; it is a smooth separated connected curve of dimension one, so the smooth-connected-curve local-ring theorem says $\mathcal O_{\widetilde X,y_i}$ is a DVR. The DVR-completion theorem makes $R_i$ a complete DVR. The local-completion residue-field theorem and Step 1 identify its residue field with $k$, with the given $k$-algebra structure. The map $H\to R_i$ is local and induces the identity on this residue field, since it is the completion of the local structural stalk map.

source.place: Tag 0C1R (lemma-prepare-delta-invariant), (5), (8), and the proof of Tag 0C3V; algebra.tex Tag 07N9; more-algebra.tex Tag 0AP1 (lemma-completion-dvr).

proof.text: Choose a uniformizer $t_i$ of $R_i$. The local-completion residue-field theorem says the maximal ideal of $R_i$ is $\mathfrak m_{y_i}R_i$, which is $t_iR_i$ since $R_i$ is a DVR; the completion-modulo-ideal theorem makes $R_i$ complete for $\mathfrak m_{y_i}R_i=t_iR_i$. The continuous power-series evaluation theorem gives a $k$-algebra map $k[[T]]\to R_i$ sending $T$ to $t_i$. It is bijective by the following direct expansion. For $r\in R_i$, successively take its residue $a_0\in k$, divide $r-a_0$ by $t_i$, take the next residue $a_1$, and continue. Completeness gives $r=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nt_i^n$. Uniqueness follows because a nonzero series with first nonzero coefficient $a_N$ evaluates to $t_i^N$ times an element with nonzero residue; the latter is a unit and $R_i$ is a domain. Identify $C$ with $D=\prod_{i=1}^b k[[t_i]]$ by these maps; its coordinate residue maps are constant coefficients.

source.place: Tag 07NL (lemma-power-series-ring-over-Cohen-fs), universal property of power series used in its proof; explicit uniformizer expansion in a complete DVR.

proof.text: Let $\rho:D\to k^b$ take constant coefficients and let $\Delta k\subset k^b$ be the diagonal. By Step 4, $\rho(H)=\Delta k$: containment follows from the local residue maps, and equality from the diagonal constants in the $k$-algebra $H$. Thus, for $P=\rho^{-1}(\Delta k)$, the induced map $D/H\to k^b/\Delta k$ is surjective with kernel $P/H$. Since $\dim_k(D/H)=\delta$, this gives $\delta\ge b-1$, with equality exactly when $P/H=0$, that is $H=P$. Here $\dim_k(k^b/\Delta k)=b-1$ because $b\ge1$.

source.place: Appendix B, printed pp. 56--57, the residue-map proof of the delta/branch inequality; written here for the completed normalization.

proof.text: The ring $P$ is explicitly the coordinate-axes ring $R_b=k[[T_1,\ldots,T_b]]/(T_iT_j\mid i\ne j)$. Indeed evaluate a series on each separate coordinate axis. Its images have the same constant coefficient. Conversely a tuple $(c+t_if_i(t_i))_i$ is the image of $c+\sum_iT_if_i(T_i)$. The kernel consists exactly of the series having zero constant coefficient and zero coefficients on all monomials supported on a single variable. Every remaining monomial is divisible by $T_iT_j$ for some $i<j$. Assign each such monomial to its first two positive indices; grouping into the finitely many pairs $(i,j)$ writes the entire series as $\sum_{i<j}T_iT_jg_{ij}$, proving ideal membership even for infinite series. For $b=1$ the kernel is zero. Hence $H=P$ implies $H\cong R_b$.

source.place: Appendix B, printed pp. 56--57, the completed ordinary-point ring; explicit coefficient calculation replacing the gluing assertion.

proof.text: For the converse, compute the normalization of the concrete subring $P\subset D$ from Step 7. The coordinate idempotents $e_1,\ldots,e_b$ generate $D$ as a $P$-module: a tuple equals its tuple of constants plus an element of $P$, and $1=\sum_ie_i$. Hence $D$ is integral over $P$ by the finite-algebra integrality theorem. Put $s=(t_1,\ldots,t_b)\in P$. It is a non-zero-divisor, $sD\subset P$, and $P[1/s]=D[1/s]=\prod_i k((t_i))$: every nonzero one-variable series is $t_i^n$ times a unit. A non-zero-divisor of $P$ has every coordinate nonzero (otherwise it annihilates the nonzero tuple supported in that coordinate with entry $t_i$). Therefore this product of fields is precisely $Q(P)$. Each $k[[t_i]]$ is integrally closed in its fraction field by the power-series normal-domain theorem applied to the field $k$. Projecting a monic equation shows $D$ is integrally closed in $Q(P)$. Since $D$ is integral over $P$, and every element integral over $P$ is also integral over $D$, the integral closure of $P$ is exactly $D$. Moreover $D/P\cong k^b/\Delta k$ by $\rho$.

source.place: Tag 0BI0 (lemma-power-series-over-Noetherian-normal-domain); finite-module integrality and the explicit coordinate-axes calculation for Temkin Appendix B.

proof.text: If $H\cong R_b$, Step 7 identifies this ring with $P$. A ring isomorphism preserves non-zero-divisors and monic equations, so extends to the total fraction rings and identifies their integral closures. Steps 3 and 8 therefore identify the pair $(C,H)$, as $k$-algebras, with $(D,P)$. It follows that $\delta=\dim_k(C/H)=\dim_k(D/P)=b-1$. Together with Steps 6--7 this proves both directions of the claimed equality criterion.

source.place: Appendix B, printed pp. 56--57, equality characterization; the normalization invariance is explicit through fractions and monic equations.

proof.text: When $x$ is smooth, Step 2 gives $M=0$, hence $\delta=0$; the inequality and $b\ge1$ force $b=1$, and the equality criterion gives $H\cong k[[T]]$. Conversely an ordinary one-fold point has this completed ring. A one-variable power-series ring is regular of dimension one by the power-series regularity theorem; regularity descends to $A$ by the completion-regularity theorem. On an affine finite-type chart with residue field $k$, the regularity/smoothness criterion now makes $x$ smooth. Thus ordinary one-fold points are exactly smooth points, and all have $\delta=0$.

The completed-geometric-local-ring definition of a node, stated in the nodal-point criterion, is here a ring isomorphism $\varphi:H\cong k[[u,v]]/(uv)=R_2$, because $k$ is already algebraically closed. Its normalization has exactly two local factors by Step 8. Step 4 identifies the normalization of $H$ with a product of $b$ local domains; the number of factors is intrinsic, since their coordinate idempotents are exactly the nonzero idempotents which cannot be written as a sum of two nonzero orthogonal idempotents. As in Step 9 (which uses only ring structure), $\varphi$ carries $C$ onto $D$; so a node has $b=2$. Moreover $\varphi$ induces a bijection of $H$-submodules of $C/H$ with $P$-submodules of $D/P\cong k^2/\Delta k$, which is one-dimensional over the residue field $k$ of $P$, hence simple. So $C/H$ is a simple $H$-module; as the residue field of $H$ is $k$ via the structure map, $\delta=\dim_k(C/H)=1=b-1$, and the equality criterion of Steps 6--7 gives a $k$-algebra isomorphism $H\cong R_2$: a node is an ordinary two-fold point. Conversely a $k$-algebra isomorphism $H\cong R_2$ is in particular a ring isomorphism, so an ordinary two-fold point is a node by that definition, with $\delta=b-1=1$.
